description: We are building AstroGuard AI for the Astronaut Health Monitoring challenge. Our team integrates predictive offline-first analytics, NASA life sciences data, and real-time computer vision (facial fatigue detection) to protect astronaut well-being during space missions without relying on Earth communication delays. Our roster is set and ready to build!
summary: our project is a vital and environment monitoring system paired an ai model for textile explanation  and a prediction algorithm that predicts problems before they occur
details:
Here is the submission text. It answers each of their questions in order, and everything in it is true of what we actually built.

AstroGuard AI — offline crew health monitoring for deep space

What it does

AstroGuard AI watches an astronaut's vital signs and their cabin environment, and warns them before something becomes a problem. It runs entirely on board. No cloud, no network, no call to Earth.

An ESP32 microcontroller reads three sensors — a MAX30102 for heart rate and blood oxygen, an AD8232 for a single-lead ECG at 250 Hz, and a DHT11 for cabin temperature and humidity — and streams them over USB to a laptop as plain text lines. A Python backend turns every value into one shared reading format, classifies it against limits from a config file, and pushes the result to a browser dashboard over a WebSocket. The dashboard shows live tiles, a scrolling ECG strip, trend charts and an alert panel, in green, yellow and red, with the status also written as a word (NOMINAL, CAUTION, ALERT, NO DATA) so it is readable at a distance and for colour-blind viewers.

Three things sit on top of that base, and they are the point of the project:

  1. A second, independent heart rate derived from the ECG. If the finger sensor loses contact, that tile goes NO DATA while the ECG-derived one keeps reporting. Two independent measurements agreeing is worth more than one.
  2. Trend forecasts. A least-squares line through the last 30 seconds of each signal is projected forward. When it would cross a limit, the dashboard raises a WATCH: "Heart Rate rising, expected to pass 110 bpm in about 35 s". Measured on our own test case, the WATCH appeared about a minute before the real alert.
  3. A Pattern Score. Fixed thresholds judge each signal alone. This score compares the whole body state — every value and its rate of change — against a baseline learned from that specific astronaut, as a z-score distance scaled 0 to 100. It catches combinations where every individual reading is still legal: heart rate 105, SpO2 94.5, cabin 26.5 °C, humidity 68. In our test, the Pattern Score raised CAUTION at 81 seconds while every other signal stayed NOMINAL the whole time.

A fourth layer explains the alerts. A local language model, running through Ollama on the same laptop, writes two plain sentences and a suggested check under each alert: "Your heart rate is higher than normal, at 143 bpm. Please check your sensor contact to ensure it is secure and not obstructed." The model never decides anything. It receives alerts the rule engine has already made, and the application never reads a level or a number back out of its text. If the model is missing or slow, the alert is unaffected and the panel simply says no explanation is available.

A webcam adds fatigue: MediaPipe face landmarks give the share of time the eyes are open, mean blink duration, and yawns per minute, computed over rolling windows and only from frames where the head is actually facing the camera. The astronaut is never asked to look at the lens. When too few usable frames arrive, the tiles say NO DATA rather than guessing.

Why it matters

On the Space Station, Earth does the watching. Telemetry reaches the ground continuously and a flight surgeon can speak to the crew within seconds. On the way to Mars, a radio signal takes about twenty minutes each way, so asking a question and getting an answer costs most of an hour, and there may be no physician on board at all. The current model of crew health monitoring does not survive the distance.

Nothing goes wrong suddenly either. Fatigue builds over days of broken sleep. Cabin CO2 creeps up, bringing headaches and poorer decisions long before any alarm. The body drifts slowly away from what is normal for that person. By the time a reading crosses an alarm limit, the problem started hours ago. A system that only compares numbers to fixed thresholds is always late, and it is always silent about what it noticed and why.

AstroGuard AI is our answer to that: it works alone, it warns early, and it explains itself. The same three properties apply to a submarine, a polar station, a mine rescue team or a rural clinic — anywhere monitoring has to be local because help is not.

Real NASA data

We did not want to demonstrate on invented numbers, so the replay mode runs the whole dashboard on real NASA recordings:

  • NASA Crew State Monitoring — real human ECG at 256 Hz from a pilot study, with an induced startle event marked in the file.
  • NASA OSDR Environmental Data App — real ISS cabin temperature, humidity and CO2, three days of the RR-1 mission.
  • NASA RadLab — real ISS absorbed radiation dose rate from the DosTel1 detector in the Columbus module, one full day.
  • NASA-STD-3001 Volume 2, through the OCHMO technical brief TB-003 "Habitable Atmosphere" — the actual cabin atmosphere limits, which are what our environment thresholds are set to rather than numbers we chose.

The real data crosses those limits on its own. ISS CO2 rises above 3950 ppm and raises a CAUTION, and every pass through the South Atlantic Anomaly takes the radiation past 200 µGy/h, roughly every ninety minutes. So the demonstration of forecasting, alerting and explanation happens on genuine ISS telemetry without us pressing anything.

How we built it

Hardware: an ESP32 DevKit (ESP-32D, CH340 USB-serial), a MAX30102 over I2C, an AD8232 single-lead ECG front end, and a DHT11, programmed in the Arduino IDE in C++. A hardware timer samples the ECG every 4 ms into a ring buffer independent of the main loop, and samples are sent in batches of ten so the serial link stays at about 1.5 kB/s of the 11 kB/s available.

Software: Python 3.14, FastAPI with a WebSocket, and a plain HTML/CSS/JavaScript dashboard with uPlot for the charts. MediaPipe Face Landmarker for the camera. Ollama with Llama 3.2 3B for the explanations, chosen from a preference list so a machine with a better GPU automatically picks the larger Llama 3.1 8B model instead. Everything is vendored into the repository: the charting library, the face model, the ISS recordings. Nothing is fetched from the internet while the system runs, which is the whole premise.

What we considered along the way

Anomaly detection without a black box. We built an Isolation Forest first, as the obvious machine-learning choice, and measured it against a plain z-score distance on the same data. The forest ranked the cases correctly but its scores were compressed — our subtle combination reached 24 out of 100 and a heart rate of 140 only reached 30, well below the alert line, and in a live run it never alerted at all. The z-score method scored both at 100 while ordinary noise sat around 15. It is also explainable in one sentence. We removed the machine-learning library entirely. Choosing the simpler method because we measured it, not because it was easier, is the decision we are most pleased with.

The language model must not be in the loop. Every alert is produced by deterministic rules with limits from a config file. The model is a narrator with no authority. This was a design rule from the start, not a safety feature bolted on, and it means a hallucination can produce a clumsy sentence but never a wrong status.

Silence is better than a guess. Every module refuses to report when it cannot be sure. The ECG heart rate has three separate gates that stop pure noise from producing a plausible-looking number — without them, random noise produced a steady fake rate. The Pattern Score publishes nothing while a sensor is missing. The fatigue tiles go NO DATA rather than averaging too few frames. A monitoring system that invents a number is worse than one that admits it does not know.

Baselines must be learned from calm. Our first Pattern Score learned its baseline while a simulated tachycardia was running, so it learned the emergency as normal and then failed to flag a real one. Baseline learning now pauses whenever any signal is not nominal, and the tile says so.

Forecasts must not cry wolf. Our first forecaster projected the recovery after every event as a straight line and announced heart rates about to fall below 50 bpm while the heart rate was settling comfortably at 72. It now compares the most recent quarter of the window against the quarter before it, so it sees a trend flattening and says nothing.

Every setting is in one config file. Thresholds, windows, sensor calibration, limits, colours, model preferences. There are no hardcoded numbers in the code, so adapting the system to a different crew member, a different sensor, or a different vehicle is an edit to one text file.

Three interchangeable data sources. Serial from real hardware, replay of recorded data, and a simulator with scripted abnormal events, all producing the same reading format, all switchable from the keyboard while the system is running. No module anywhere knows where its data came from. That is what lets us demonstrate a medical emergency to judges without anyone having to have one.

Two notes before you paste it: if there is a character limit, the sections that cut cleanly are "What we considered along the way" (keep the first two items) and the hardware paragraph. And one honest caveat — the AD8232 electrodes have not yet produced a clean trace on the real board, so if a judge asks what is working on hardware, the answer is the DHT11 and the MAX30102 live over serial, with the ECG path proven on the real NASA recording through the replay source.
